title: Where food is first broken
q: Where does chewing mechanically break food into smaller pieces?
why: Chewing in the mouth mechanically breaks food into smaller pieces and increases exposed surface area.

title: Where starch digestion can start
q: In which part of the digestive tract can salivary amylase begin breaking down starch?
why: Salivary amylase can begin starch digestion in the mouth. Further carbohydrate digestion occurs later in the small intestine.

title: Moving a swallowed bolus
q: Which tube uses peristaltic contractions to move a swallowed bolus toward the stomach?
why: The esophagus moves the swallowed bolus toward the stomach using coordinated muscular contractions called peristalsis.

title: An acidic digestive compartment
q: In which organ do parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into digestive contents?
why: Parietal cells in gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid into the stomach. The stomach also has protective mechanisms for its lining.

title: Protein digestion begins
q: In which organ does pepsin begin breaking dietary proteins into smaller peptides?
why: Pepsin acts in the acidic stomach to break proteins into smaller polypeptides. Protein digestion continues in the small intestine.

title: Where most absorption happens
q: In which part of the human digestive tract does most nutrient absorption take place?
why: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine, whose folds and villi increase the surface available for absorption.

title: Recovering remaining water
q: Which part of the digestive tract absorbs much of the water remaining in material that has passed through the small intestine?
why: The large intestine absorbs much of the remaining water and electrolytes from material entering it. Much water was already absorbed in the small intestine.

title: Microbes and dietary fiber
q: Where can gut microbes ferment some dietary fibers that escaped digestion in the small intestine?
why: Microbes in the large intestine can ferment some undigested dietary fibers, producing metabolites including short-chain fatty acids. Different fibers are fermented to different extents.

title: A digestive fluid is produced
q: Which organ produces bile for delivery to the small intestine?
why: The liver produces bile, which can be stored and concentrated in the gallbladder before delivery to the duodenum.

title: A digestive fluid is stored
q: Which organ normally stores and concentrates bile made by the liver?
why: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile. It is the liver, not the gallbladder, that produces the bile.

title: A buffer reaches the gut
q: Which organ supplies bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice to the duodenum?
why: The pancreas delivers bicarbonate-containing juice to the duodenum, helping neutralize acidic contents arriving from the stomach.

title: Enzymes arrive from a neighbor
q: Which accessory organ produces pancreatic amylase, lipase and protease precursors for delivery to the small intestine?
why: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and enzyme precursors that enter the small intestine in pancreatic juice.

title: A meeting point for fluids
q: Bile and pancreatic juice normally enter the duodenum. Which part of the digestive tract is the duodenum?
why: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine and receives bile and pancreatic juice through ducts.

title: A sugar leaves the gut
q: After intestinal cells absorb glucose, which vascular route normally receives it for transport toward the liver?
why: Absorbed glucose enters blood capillaries in intestinal villi and travels toward the liver through the hepatic portal circulation.

title: A different route for fat
q: After long-chain lipid products are packaged into chylomicrons inside intestinal cells, which route normally receives them first?
why: Chylomicrons enter lymphatic capillaries called lacteals before reaching the bloodstream. Short-chain fatty acids can follow a different route.
